title: Governments made 283 promises to protect children. Manila’s test is what gets funded
subtitle: A global conference has produced new commitments on violence at home, in schools and online. For children and their caregivers, the crucial questions concern budgets, deadlines and access to help.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Governments from 94 countries made 283 pledges to tackle violence against children at a global conference in Manila on 18–19 November, according to UNICEF. The commitments include spending promises, proposed legal changes and targets for safer schools. They are undertakings for future action, not evidence that children are already safer.

The distinction matters because this was the second ministerial gathering in a process launched in Bogotá in November 2024. Another conference can strengthen political accountability. Counting promises alone cannot show whether a child who reports abuse will find a trained worker, a safe place or continuing support.

The Philippines hosted the meeting with UNICEF and the World Health Organization, working with the UN Special Representative on Violence against Children. Its outcome offers families and campaigners a set of commitments against which to question their governments.
From a pledge to a service

Tanzania pledged to invest US$190 million in child protection by 2029, UNICEF’s account of the conference says. Nepal committed to halving violence in schools by 2030. Burundi promised a ban on corporal punishment by 2028. These are different kinds of commitments: a funding figure, an outcome target and a proposed change in law.

Each needs a different test. A spending pledge requires an identifiable budget and evidence that money reaches services. A reduction target needs a credible starting measure and repeat measurement. A legal ban needs implementation, including support for adults to change harmful behaviour and a route for children to obtain protection.

That is an accountability framework, not a finding that these governments have failed their new promises. The announcements reviewed for this article do not establish that the pledged money has been disbursed or the targets achieved.

UNICEF deputy executive director Ted Chaiban put the financing problem plainly in prepared remarks for the meeting: “a pledge without an implementation pathway or a budget is a promise a child cannot use.” He urged governments to prioritise child protection in national budgets and involve finance ministries.

His intervention also described what implementation should look like: help for parents before violence occurs, safer schools and a rapid response from trained professionals when children need protection and recovery. These are services with staffing and recurring costs, not simply awareness campaigns.
Protection cannot stop at the front door

The scale of the problem extends well beyond highly publicised criminal cases. UNICEF estimates that 1.6 billion children experience violent discipline at home. That term includes psychological aggression as well as physical punishment; it should not be read as a count of children experiencing one particular form of assault.

The agency also estimates that 610 million children live with mothers who experienced intimate-partner violence in the preceding year. This is a different measure, with possible overlap, not another population to add to the first figure. It underlines why children’s safety and their mothers’ safety cannot be treated as unrelated policy problems.

These are estimates describing existing conditions, not new incidents recorded at the Manila conference. They help explain the breadth of the task without providing a scorecard for any individual country’s latest pledge.

For women caring for children, the practical question is whether protection systems can respond to the household’s circumstances. A school referral is of limited use if the receiving service has no capacity. An instruction to report harm needs to be accompanied by a safe, accessible way to do so.

WHO’s announcement before the meeting framed prevention as a government responsibility across homes, schools and digital spaces. The final commitments should therefore be assessed across institutions, rather than leaving parents or teachers individually responsible for delivering a national promise.
What children should be able to ask next

The most useful follow-up to Manila would be public reporting that names the responsible agency, the funding available, the deadline and the progress made. Children and caregivers should be able to understand that information without interpreting a diplomatic declaration.

They should also have a role in judging whether services are usable. A programme can exist on paper while remaining difficult to reach, frightening to approach or unable to provide sustained help. Reporting activity and reporting children’s experience are different tasks; both matter.

Manila has supplied new promises. ATHENA’s test is whether those commitments become dependable protection in ordinary life: at home, in a classroom and when a child asks an adult for help. The responsibility to make that happen belongs to the institutions making the pledges, not to the children waiting for them.
The Athena Perspective.
